An eruption is a sudden, forceful burst or release of something that has been building up inside — something that was contained, under pressure, or hidden, and then breaks out powerfully and often violently.

Think of it this way: you shake a soda bottle for a while, and the moment you open the cap, the liquid explodes outward. That explosive release is the idea behind an eruption.

The word is used in several different situations, but the same core idea runs through all of them.

1. Volcanic Eruption (the most well-known use)

This is what most people picture first. When a volcano erupts, enormous amounts of lava, ash, smoke, and hot gases are violently ejected from the volcano's opening. These materials had been building up under intense pressure deep inside the Earth, and when they finally break through the surface, that event — or the result of that event — is called an eruption.

The eruption of Mount St. Helens in 1980 was one of the most destructive in American history.

Key things to note:

  • "Eruption" can refer to the act of erupting (the moment it happens).
  • It can also refer to the entire episode of volcanic activity (which can last hours, days, or even years).

2. Skin Eruption (medical use)

In medicine and everyday health talk, an eruption refers to the sudden appearance of spots, rashes, blisters, or sores on the skin. Just like a volcano, something is "breaking out" through the surface — in this case, through the skin.

The doctor noticed an eruption of red spots across the patient's arms.

A skin eruption can be caused by allergies, infections, or certain medications.

You might also hear doctors call a rash a "cutaneous eruption" — "cutaneous" just means "of the skin."

3. Eruption of Emotion, Sound, or Reaction

This is a figurative use — meaning it's not literal, but it borrows the volcano idea to describe human behavior or events.

When a sudden, explosive, uncontainable outburst happens — of anger, laughter, cheering, violence, conflict, or noise — it can be called an eruption.

There was an eruption of laughter in the room when he told the joke.

The referee's decision caused an eruption of anger among the fans.

The peaceful protest turned into an eruption of violence.

The suggestion is always the same: something was brewing or building, and then it broke out all at once, with force.

4. Eruption of Teeth (dental use)

This is a specific but common medical use. When a baby's teeth push through the gums for the first time — or when adult teeth come in — that process is called tooth eruption.

The eruption of the first molars usually happens around the age of six.

Again, the idea is the same: something hidden and growing finally breaks through a surface.

No matter the context, every use of the word eruption contains the same building blocks:

  • Something was building up (pressure, heat, infection, emotion, tension).
  • It was contained or hidden (inside a volcano, under the skin, beneath the surface of calm).
  • It suddenly and forcefully broke through (outward, onto the surface, into the open).

That three-part pattern — building up → being held in → bursting out — is the soul of the word.
Eruption vs. Explosion (a subtle but important difference)

Both words suggest a sudden, violent release, but:

  • Explosion typically involves a single, instantaneous blast — it happens in a split second.
  • Eruption often implies a process — something pouring, flowing, or breaking out over a period of time, not just one instant. A volcanic eruption can last weeks. A skin eruption can persist for days.

That said, in casual use, people sometimes use them interchangeably when talking about emotions or crowd reactions, and that's perfectly fine.

Eruption = the sudden, forceful bursting out of something (lava, rashes, emotion, teeth) that had been building up or held inside. It almost always carries a sense of intensity, power, and something that could not be contained any longer.
